== Biography ==
'''Cookstown family extension, 17 October 2026:''' The Mitchell-family [[Glasgow-1970|James Glasgow]] is an '''uncertain working son''' of this older pedigree account, conditional on the existing possible Corvanaghan/Moneymore identities. The reviewed 1759 index says '''Drumcarn''', names no kin and does not identify this profile or prove the father choice.<ref name="CookstownGortinReview" />
'''James Glasgow''' was born about '''1700'''. His birth date is an estimate. No record has yet been found establishing his birthplace, parents, wife or children.

An Irish probate index includes an entry for '''James Glasgow of Drumearn, County Tyrone''', in '''1759'''.<ref>"Cavan, County Armagh, Ireland records," images, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QS7-L94F-MWB5?view=index : accessed 26 March 2025), image 76 of 127.</ref>

The WikiTree source currently associated with the profile appears to give the more precise date '''17 January 1759'''. The meaning of that date has not yet been confirmed. It may represent:

* the date on which the will was written;
* the date of probate;
* the date of administration;
* the date of an associated bond; or
* the date on which the record was entered in the index.

The separate probate transcription reviewed in July 2026 supplies only the year 1759. The full date should therefore be retained only as an indexed record date, not automatically treated as the date of death.

The agreement in name, exact residence and year makes the 1759 probate entry a strong match to this profile. It establishes Drumearn as James’s documented residence at the time of the estate proceeding. It does not prove that Drumearn was his birthplace or place of death.

James probably died before the relevant probate or administration action was completed in 1759, although the precise nature and date of that action remain to be confirmed.

== Drumearn and Derryloran Records ==

The 1740 Protestant householders return for Derryloran parish records two householders named '''James Glasgow''' and two named '''William Glasgow'''. The return does not give their townlands or state any relationships between them.

These entries provide evidence for a Glasgow family cluster in Derryloran by 1740, but neither James can presently be identified with this profile.

The 1766 religious census for Derryloran parish records:

* two men named '''James Glasgo''' at Drumearn; and
* one '''John Glasgo''' at Drumearn.

If the 1759 entry represents probate or administration following this James’s death, the two men named James in 1766 cannot be him. They were probably younger relatives or unrelated namesakes within the same local Glasgow cluster.

The 1766 entries demonstrate continued Glasgow residence at Drumearn, but they do not identify the later householders as James’s sons, grandsons, nephews or other relatives.

The same will-index page also includes an entry for '''William Glasgow of Killycooragh, County Tyrone''', dated '''17 December 1770'''. No relationship between William and James has been established. Similarity of surname, county and probate context is not sufficient to attach William as a son or other relative.

== Distinction from Other Men Named James Glasgow ==

This James should not presently be merged with [[Glasgow-2988|James Glasgow (abt.1720-)]], who was recorded at '''Corvanaghan''' in Kildress parish in 1766.

Corvanaghan and Drumearn are separate townlands in different parishes. The difference in residence, together with the apparent 1759 estate proceeding for the Drumearn James, supports treating them as distinct men unless a direct record proves otherwise.

This profile should also not automatically be identified with either of the two unnamed-townland James Glasgow householders recorded in Derryloran in 1740. One of those men may have been the Drumearn testator, but the surviving return does not provide enough information to determine which one.

== Family and Relationship Research ==

No inspected record identifies James’s parents, wife or children.

The probate index supplies his name, Drumearn residence and the year 1759, but the available transcription does not name:

* a widow;
* children;
* executors or administrators;
* beneficiaries;
* witnesses;
* sureties; or
* property inherited by later Glasgow residents.

Claims that James lived at Moneymore, was born in County Tyrone or fathered particular later members of the Glasgow family require separate evidence.

The presence of Glasgow householders at Drumearn in 1766 makes a family connection plausible, but no specific relationship should be created from surname and locality alone.

== Y-DNA Research ==

James is the earliest currently identified ancestor in the paternal line of a Y-DNA relative of [[Glasgow-933|M Glasgow]].

The reported comparison is five differences over 660 markers. This result may support a relationship within a wider Glasgow paternal line, but it does not identify:

* the generation at which the lines connect;
* the common ancestor;
* this James as the ancestor of another documented Glasgow line; or
* either 1766 Drumearn householder as his son.

Y-DNA evidence should be used alongside documentary evidence rather than as a substitute for it.

== Research Priorities ==

Further research should establish:

* what the date 17 January 1759 represents;
* the precise probate court or index series involved;
* whether the original will, probate record, administration record or bond survives;
* whether a pre-destruction abstract of the record exists;
* the names of any beneficiaries, executors, administrators, witnesses or sureties;
* whether property at Drumearn passed to a later Glasgow;
* whether either James Glasgo recorded at Drumearn in 1766 can be linked to the estate;
* whether John Glasgo of Drumearn in 1766 was related to the testator;
* whether either 1740 Derryloran householder named James Glasgow can be associated with Drumearn; and
* whether the 1770 William Glasgow of Killycooragh appears in any connected deed, will or administration record.

An online family tree for a James Glasgow is available at:

* [https://gw.geneanet.org/moodyfh?n=glasgow&oc=1&p=james Archived or supplementary source]
Information from online family trees should be independently verified against contemporary records.

== Research Conclusion ==

The 1759 probate entry for '''James Glasgow of Drumearn, County Tyrone''' is a strong match to this profile because the name, exact residence and terminal year agree.

It supports Drumearn as his documented residence and 1759 as the year of an estate or probate proceeding. The exact significance of 17 January 1759 remains unresolved, and the date should not yet be used as a certain date of death.

If the 1759 entry followed James’s death, the two men named James Glasgo at Drumearn in the 1766 religious census were later namesakes or members of a younger generation.

No record presently proves James’s birthplace, death place, parents, wife, children or relationship to the 1740 and 1766 Derryloran householders, William Glasgow of Killycooragh or James Glasgow of Corvanaghan.

== Research Notes ==
=== Killycurragh generations, 20 October 2026 ===

The freshly read published transcription of PRONI T1959/3 distinguishes an older William of Killycurragh, the writer’s paternal great-grandfather, from his son William, the writer’s paternal grandfather and husband of Miss Cunningham. The younger William is the Cunningham husband, whose sons included James and Samuel. His son John married Margaret Glasgow after ordination at Coleraine and died at his father’s house in Orritor in July 1801. The surviving child, the anonymous writer, was born five months later; Margaret died in 1817. The separate church compilation identifies John Glasgow from Orritor, ordained at New Row, Coleraine, on 8 March 1796 and dead on 13 July 1801. The shared ministry, origin, name and death month strongly identify the husband. The writer separately describes Margaret’s father William as a son of James Glasgow and Margaret Rutherford; the two parental lines must not be collapsed into one grandfather.

Select [[Glasgow-1318|William Glasgow]] as the possible father of the letter-defined Cunningham husband at 36%. The letter supplies an older Killycurragh William, son of the Tullycoll/Tullyall William and brother of James (husband of Margaret Rutherford) and John (husband of Anne Mason). The 1705 Kirknewton child William has a named father William and a generation compatible with being grandfather of the minister ordained in 1796. The 1702 John baptism supplies a compatible second named son in that Scottish father cluster; the existing James-1025 family supplies the Irish James comparison. This is a positive but non-exclusive family-cluster hypothesis. The Scottish child’s adult identity and migration remain unproved. The 36% includes that identity uncertainty; it is not a confident Scottish–Irish bridge.

Select the letter-defined William of Killycurragh as Rev. John Glasgow’s father at 94% (strongly supported). The writer explicitly gives the writer’s father John, the writer’s paternal grandfather William and his Cunningham marriage. John’s Coleraine ordination, Orritor origin and July 1801 death match the separate New Row minister entry. This concerns the minister’s record-defined identity; it does not identify his grandfather with a Scottish baptism or upgrade his brothers’ later-profile matches.

Select [[Glasgow-2426|William Glasgow]] as Margaret Glasgow’s probable father at 84%. That profile represents William, son of [[Glasgow-1025|James Glasgow]] and Margaret Rutherford, which matches the letter’s maternal-grandfather family position. The letter explicitly names the eldest daughter Margaret as the minister’s wife and the writer’s mother. The profile’s circa-1735 birth and circa-1829 United States death are inherited claims, not exclusionary records and not corrected here. The letter calls William an eldest son; the circa-1735 estimate conflicts with the earlier estimated births of his attached brothers. Those unverified estimates require checking and are preserved here. This is the maternal grandfather, distinct from the Cunningham husband. Original records and an independent adult-life bridge remain to be found.

These are exact subjective assessments of complete relationship-and-identity propositions, not measured probabilities. The family letter is undated and unsigned and is read through Albert Rutherford’s published transcription of a photocopy, not an inspected PRONI original. The minister list is a derivative compilation whose independence from the family tradition is unproved. The Scottish adult identities remain possible: neither the letter nor the 1705 baptism supplies a migration, occupation, property or witness bridge between Kirknewton and Tyrone. The letter’s three-son family and second-cousin statement are internally consistent clues from one source, not independent corroborations. Existing people, vital fields and mothers are preserved. Miss Cunningham and Anne Rutherford are reported maternal names, not transferred to existing maternal profiles. The letter’s first-settler story is family tradition, not proof of the first Glasgow in Tyrone or of the surname’s origin.<ref name="KillycurraghGenerations20261020">PRONI T1959/3, [https://www.genealogy.com/forum/surnames/topics/rutherford/5445/ published transcription], read 20 October 2026; original uninspected. [https://cotyrone.com/churchrecord/ministers-pres.html Minister compilation], John Glasgow, New Row; derivative entry, not an original register.</ref>

=== Cookstown–Gortin family review — 17 October 2026 ===

Select the older [[Glasgow-1025|James Glasgow]] account as the Cookstown progenitor [[Glasgow-1970|James Glasgow]]’s uncertain working father, conditional on the existing Corvanaghan/Moneymore family model. The c.1700 and c.1730 estimates allow a father–son generation. [[Glasgow-1970|James]] is already a surviving possible identity for the Cookstown-area Corvanaghan [[Glasgow-2988|James]], whose selected working father is [[Glasgow-1025|James]] through the separate Moneymore comparison. Extending that same unproved pedigree gives the Mitchell account a consistent, revisable place in the broader family. The district context comes from those Cookstown/Corvanaghan/Moneymore comparisons, not from the 1759 index. This is an inherited family hypothesis with no independent father record for the Mitchell progenitor.

No will, lease or baptism names the Cookstown James as the older James’s son. The reviewed PRONI detail says Drumcarn, County Tyrone, not Drumearn, and gives 17 January 1759 without age or kin; the modern profile identity and meaning of that date remain unresolved. It cannot corroborate Drumearn residence, a death date, or this father choice. The older and younger James accounts may themselves be duplicates rather than separate generations; if established, the father edge must collapse. The existing older pedigree and the Corvanaghan/Moneymore identity remain unproved. The 1879 history reports Scotland-to-Cookstown migration about 1750, while the older James’s profile is placed in Tyrone; neither a return journey nor that Scottish birthplace is established here. Multiple James and William householders appear in the 1740 Derryloran return, and two James men appear at Drumearn in 1766. William or another local father, a collateral link and a separate Scottish origin remain alternatives. Mary Harkness is not transferred to the Mitchell account, and Margaret Rutherford is not assigned as its mother. [[Glasgow-1970|James]], [[Glasgow-2988|James]], [[Glasgow-1024|James]] and the older [[Glasgow-1025|James]] remain separate possible overlapping reconstructions, not independently proved sons or households.

Two uncertain working father links join the previously detached 6-profile Cookstown family and 17-profile Gortin family to the main working tree. The 23 are retained pre-1850 profile accounts, including unresolved possible duplicates, not 23 newly discovered or independently verified people. Motherhood and marriage grades apply only to the named Hillsdale core; no mother, spouse, birth/death change, new person or merge is added elsewhere. All raw WikiTree family fields remain intact and no live save is made. The working connectivity gain measures selected hypotheses, while confidently marked connectivity remains unchanged. This batch reuses maintained source reviews and makes no new original-page inspection claim. === Selected uncertain family — 16 October 2026 ===

[[Glasgow-1025|James Glasgow, older family account]] is selected as the very uncertain working father of [[Glasgow-2988|James Glasgow of Corvanaghan]], the 1766 Corvanaghan householder, through preferred provisional identity with [[Glasgow-1024|James Glasgow of Moneymore]] of Moneymore. The existing Corvanaghan biography already retains the Moneymore man as a compatible candidate: the places are roughly nine miles apart, the name matches and their circa 1720/1722 births are estimates rather than a real two-year conflict. The 1766 Irish occurrence can precede the compiled 1770 immigration claim associated with the Moneymore family; no post 1766 Irish occurrence has been assigned to the Corvanaghan man. This is a weak locality and chronology preference, not proof of emigration or identity. The older James is already an uncertain father in the Moneymore pedigree. Extending that attachment gives the Corvanaghan account a conditional place in the same family, without inventing an intermediate generation. It inherits two major uncertainties: adult identity and the older pedigree itself.

The older James account’s circa 1700 birth would allow an ordinary father–son interval of about 20–22 years, if the estimates are close. Those guessed years do not independently establish paternity. No contemporary record names the older James as father of either Moneymore James or the Corvanaghan householder. The current older-father attachment is a tree hypothesis, not a clause in the 1766 return, the pension record or the later family history. The older and younger James accounts might themselves be duplicates rather than father and son; if that identity is established, this additional father edge must collapse with it. Their existing Scottish ancestral attachments receive no new support. No mother is selected: the uncertain Rutherford attachment on the Moneymore account is not independently supported for the Corvanaghan man and is not copied.

The 1759 will reference does not prove this father generation. The previously reviewed PRONI detail names Drumcarn, not Drumearn, and supplies no age or kin. It may concern the older account, the Moneymore James or another namesake. The meaning of 17 January 1759 and the testator’s modern profile identity remain unresolved. No 1759 death, estate event or residence is transferred to the 1766 Corvanaghan householder. The older profile’s structured dates and places are retained as existing fields with those qualifications; the new parent model does not resolve them.

Faris’s later genealogy calls [[Glasgow-12|Glasgow-12]]’s father James of Moneymore, but the underlying evidence for that father identification has not been inspected. Robert’s 1834 pension declaration gives County Derry birth in 1749 and arrival in Virginia in 1769; it does not name parents or siblings. The fuller Mary Harkness and sibling package, the compiled 1770 entry and the 1804 same-name naturalisation applicant remain separate inherited claims. The reported departure of a mother and elder brothers by 1766 does not independently place their father in America that year. No new wife, emigrant child, ship, naturalisation identity or extreme-age death is attached to the Corvanaghan account. The 1766 return and the later Moneymore family tradition may still concern different men.

One very uncertain father is newly selected through a possible Moneymore identity and an already uncertain older pedigree. No mother, source-proved parentage, migration, merge, vital-field change, original inspection, live WikiTree edit or confidence upgrade is claimed. The compared James accounts remain separate and may be duplicates rather than distinct brothers or generations. Working connectivity counts retained accounts and does not independently validate those identities. === Possible James Glascow, Fogs Manor postal addressee ===
James Glascow, Fogs Manor, is listed among letters remaining in the Philadelphia post office.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/39395391/ The Pennsylvania Gazette, 1757-04-07, p.1].</ref>

Fogs Manor is the printed address qualifier. A neighbouring "Phil. Co." in a separate alphabetic column is not this man’s address. The list states no occupation, so it does not identify him as the later Greenwich Packet master.

This may concern [[Glasgow-1025]]. Weak compatible 1757 chronological lead: estimated c.1700 birth and exact 17 January 1759 death allow the postal date; no address connection. Its exact 1759 death field would conflict with the 1777 active master if correctly attributed; the underlying probate identity remains unresolved.
